query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for plasma-facing applications in fusion reactors, what single intervention could improve radiation tolerance while preserving mechanical integrity and engineering practicality? Formulate one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the proposed mechanism, predicts a measurable improvement over the unmodified baseline, defines the conditions under which the effect should hold, cites prior evidence supporting the causal rationale, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor fraction (around 5 atomic %) of Mn to a refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a BCC TaNbHfZr alloy) will improve its radiation tolerance by increasing lattice distortion to localize defect migration and thus enhance vacancy–interstitial recombination, thereby reducing void swelling under fusion‐relevant irradiation conditions while preserving its mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., equimolar TaNbHfZr, with a simple BCC structure) as used for plasma-facing applications.
generation.intervention: Alloy the baseline R-HEA with approximately 5 atomic % Mn to form a modified composition (TaNbHfZrMn).
generation.conditions: Irradiation with energetic particles (e.g., heavy ions or neutron-relevant conditions) at elevated temperatures (roughly 0.3–0.6 Tm, for example, 773–973 K) and doses typical of plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased local lattice distortion due to Mn addition, which alters the energy landscape for defect migration.
generation.mechanism: The Mn atoms create additional lattice strain and chemical complexity. This enhanced lattice distortion is expected to confine the migration pathways of irradiation‐induced point defects (vacancies and interstitials), promoting their recombination before large voids or defect clusters can form.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the Mn-doped alloy should exhibit a measurable reduction (on the order of tens of percent, though the exact value is uncertain) in void size or density under equivalent irradiation doses while retaining similar yield strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: Unmodified refractory HEA (TaNbHfZr) irradiated under identical conditions, which shows a characteristic level of void swelling and defect cluster formation as determined by TEM or other microstructural analysis.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected under high-temperature irradiation conditions typical of fusion environments. At temperatures or doses far outside the studied range, or if excessive Mn causes phase instability, the effect may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: While similar mechanisms have been reported in other equiatomic alloys (e.g., Ni-based systems) and supported by observations of how compositional complexity alters defect migration, the exact degree of improvement and its universality in refractory HEAs remain to be experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set with the baseline refractory HEA (TaNbHfZr) and one set with the Mn-doped alloy (TaNbHfZrMn, with ~5 at% Mn). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature irradiation (e.g., using heavy-ion or neutron irradiation at 773–973 K) up to a dose typical for plasma-facing components. Use transmission electron microscopy to quantify void and defect cluster sizes/densities, and perform mechanical testing (e.g., yield strength and ductility) before and after irradiation.
measurements: Void and defect cluster morphology (size and density) via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mn-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in defect cluster size or void density (or shows increased defect accumulation) relative to the baseline, or if its mechanical properties degrade below acceptable engineering limits, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Irradiation with helium ions led to lattice shrinking in Ni and lattice expansion in NiCoFeCr and NiCoFeCrMn. The increase in the lattice parameter can be caused by the microstrain and defects generated by helium irradiation [], where point defects and small defect clusters increase the strain and lattice parameter, while larger clusters, such as dislocation loops, can reduce them []. The lattice expansion and microstrain decrease at higher irradiation temperatures, since it stimulates defect recombination, reduces the residual stress and lattice distortion, and the expansion depends not only on the irradiation conditions, but also on the constituent elements of the target [,]. The addition of Fe and Mn reduce the volume swelling in the Ni alloys []. In this study, the lattice expansion in FCC NiCoFeCrMn samples irradiated by helium ions to a dose of 23 dpa was approximately 0.35% relative to unirradiated samples, which was lower than in FCC high-entropy ceramics (WTiVNbTa)C5 irradiated by carbon ions to comparable a dose of 23 dpa at room temperature [], and lower than in BCC HEA VCrFeMn irradiated by He to 1.3 dpa at 1023 K []. The HEAs are also resistant to forming large defect clusters compared with binary nickel alloy systems and have the self-healing effect. Dislocation loops and lines can significantly affect the hardening and embrittlement, but in CrMnFeCoNi and CrFeCoNi, the density of dislocation loops after irradiation by Ni ions was higher than that of binary and ternary nickel alloys, and most of these loops had a smaller size []. The reasons for the self-healing of HEAs include high atomic stress and lattice distortion caused by the large difference in atomic size, which lead to the amorphization followed by crystallization of the alloy [,], and the similarity of vacancy and interstitial migration energies, which improve the defect annihilation []. Thus, the structural features of the HEAs affect the radiation resistance.

The integrated experimental and modelling work shows that reduced defect mobility and altered migration paths on a modified energy landscape, resulting from alloy complexity, can modify defect dynamics to promote annihilation of radiation damage that ultimately enhance radiation tolerance. Irradiation-induced void formation in nickel and Ni-containing equiatomic SP-CSAs at elevated temperature is controlled by the migration behaviours of interstitial clusters. Short-range 3D motion of interstitial clusters that significantly increases the vacancy–interstitial recombination rate plays a key role in preventing significant void swelling in NiFe, NiCoFe, NiCoFeCr and NiCoFeCrMn. The mechanism has been revealed by TEM observation and confirmed by MD simulation. Composition complexity and lattice distortion due to the alloy components effectively modify the defect migration behaviour in the equiatomic SP-CSAs. More localized migration of interstitial clusters enhances recombination of point defects in the cascade region where the defects are created.
